shortlist.raw_text: GPT-6-Astra demonstrates a level of competence in robotic manipulation and navigation that challenges the conventional paradigm of building specialized models for individual tasks and embodiments. In this report, we ask not only how capable GPT-6-Astra is, but what its capabilities imply for the field. First, we probe the limits of standalone GPT-6-Astra. We conduct a large-scale evaluation across 12 representative benchmarks spanning tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands. Under a unified protocol that allows in-context learning (ICL) from training-set demonstrations and substantially increases the number of execution steps, GPT-6-Astra achieves unprecedented performance (Fig. 1). Future research may focus on improving 1) the generality of ICL 2) cost and execution time, 3) physical-state verification, 4) recovery from irreversible failures, and 5) long-horizon preservation of progress. Second, we study the agentic harness for embodied control. We identify that close-loop coordination between a high-level "System 2" reasoner (i.e., GPT-6-Astra) and a low-level "System 1" controller (e.g., π0.5) is costly but effective. Third, we examine GPT-6-Astra on real-world deployment. Our experiments on 8 robot configurations reveal substantial gaps: 1) robot demonstrations required for ICL are expensive to collect, and 2) it is implausible to trade longer execution for higher success rates with physical constraints. Fourth, we envision the next generation of embodied benchmarks. We develop a prototype that 1) derives tasks from real-world needs, 2) provides no in-domain demonstrations, and 3) judges agents on a world clock that keeps running while they deliberate. Taken together, our results suggest that GPT-6-Astra has largely crossed the threshold of embodied competence, but not yet that of practical embodied intelligence.

shortlist.raw_text: Long-horizon agents accumulate progress in persistent task state, yet repeatedly process interaction histories describing how that progress was achieved. This raises a natural question: can long-horizon context instead be organized around reusable progress rather than the history that produced it? In this paper, we introduce CarryOn, an object-oriented context runtime that organizes continuation around reusable task objects. Rather than treating compressed histories or reconstructed accounts of progress as the primary basis for continuation, CarryOn builds a context view from continuation carriers, complementary execution context, and a live tail of recent interactions. A core challenge is keeping this reusable basis valid after its surrounding history is retired: how can CarryOn update the basis without reconstructing the full representation at every fold? CarryOn maintains carrier records across folds, revising affected records against bound evidence and applicable environment checks while carrying forward unaffected records and jointly updating execution context. Experiments on OSWorld 2.0 and BrowseComp-Plus show improved gains of 5.8% and 7.0% while reducing total token usage by 51.9% and 22.9%, respectively. Project page: https://ethannju.github.io/carryon

shortlist.raw_text: Agents built on vision language models (VLMs) now compete with learned policies on robot manipulation leaderboards. We ask how far a coding agent can go when it controls a robot instead of a computer, and where it stops. Our system, HexaShell, keeps the harness thin: it only turns the agent's commands into robot motion. The agent drives a robot with two arms through one command line. It sees three RGB cameras and knows their calibration. After each failed attempt, the agent reads the log, finds the cause, and writes or fixes small programs called tools. In this way it keeps what it learns as code, as a coding agent does when it fixes a failing test. The tools may use only what the robot observes. They use triangulation to find where objects are, relative to each other and to the gripper. If two cameras see the same point, the point lies where the two camera rays meet. If a point lies on a known plane, such as the table or the top of a block, it lies where its ray meets that plane. When the head camera is not enough, the robot moves a wrist camera to get a second view. We build the tools on only ten layouts of one seed per task, then freeze them and test them on ten new layouts of the same seed. We use Codex with GPT-6-Astra at medium reasoning effort. On all 42 RoboDojo tasks, HexaShell reaches a success rate of 39.7% and a progress score of 48.0, averaged in the same way as the leaderboard. This is a new state of the art on RoboDojo. The limit is contact, not reasoning: pushing reaches 92.5% and memory tasks 65.0%, but tight insertion only 8.3%. When the agent fails, it usually sees the failure but cannot make the motion work. We open source the tools evolved so far at https://github.com/HexaFuture/HexaShell.

shortlist.raw_text: Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.

shortlist.title: Anthropic gives outside AI watchdog “employee-like” access
shortlist.summary: The outside watchdog can publish its findings without Anthropic's approval.
shortlist.raw_text: Anthropic has granted external evaluators “employee-like access” to assess the risks of its models, following through on a commitment to increase safeguards over concerns the technology could run catastrophically out of control. METR, a nonprofit that has worked with leading labs including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, now has a team embedded in the Claude maker’s office with access to its hardware and internal systems. A greater role for third-party evaluators is among the main concrete steps the labs have proposed in response to rising concern about the dangers more capable AI systems could pose to the economy, cyber security and humanity at large. Coverage from New York Post: "Ex-U Penn professor arrested for blocking Uber Eats robot ‘taking over human jobs’"
She’s not going to let the robots take over without a fight.
A retired University of Pennsylvania professor was hauled away by cops after staging a one-woman blockade against an Uber Eats delivery robot — and she’s vowing to keep raging against the machines despite her brush with the law.
Carolyn Marvin, 78, was arrested on Wednesday after planting herself in the path an autonomous food delivery bot in Philadelphia and refusing to budge, according to Philly Voice.
Cops reportedly asked the determined senior “multiple times” to get out of the way and let the machine go about its business.
Instead of backing down, she ended up in cuffs, slapped with a disorderly conduct charge.
Her beef with the bots — they’re taking jobs from humans.
Marvin has been waging a personal war against the delivery machines for months, accusing the corporations behind them of putting flesh-and-blood workers out of business “in order to enrich their own bottom line.”
“I know they’re taking the jobs of human delivery workers and so, I have been protesting them whenever I saw them by standing in front of them and preventing them from going forward,” Marvin said.
The feisty ex-professor — who taught a class in freedom of expression at Penn — said she’s confronted sidewalk cyborgs on many occasions, and the arrest won’t stop her.
In fact, she plans to contest the charges.
“I think it’s my First Amendment right to publicly demonstrate on a sidewalk to protest against delivery robots,” Ms. Marvin told WPVI-TV.
She went on to say it’s part of being an American citizen.
“I’m exercising the rights of my citizenship, so I think of it in those terms.”
Meanwhile, her robot rebellion has sparked a battle of its own online.
“Some heroines don’t wear capes,” one admirer cheered.
But not everyone was rooting for the anti-robot crusader.
“Stopping it from bringing people they medicine is a crime!” one critic fumed.
Still, Marvin isn’t letting the backlash — or her arrest — short circuit her mission.
She says she intends to keep confronting the bots wherever she spots them, and hopes her sidewalk shenanigans will encourage people to talk about the future of human jobs.
“It allows me to talk to people about what’s going on,” she said. “It’s always very interesting conversations that we have, and I think it’s good to have those kinds of conversations in public space.”
The robots, built by tech company Avride, have been making Uber Eats deliveries in parts of Philadelphia since March.

A Philadelphia woman was arrested after repeatedly stepping in front of an Uber Eats delivery robot near Reading Terminal Market, setting off a public debate over automation, labor, and the boundaries of protest.
Carolyn Marvin was charged with disorderly conduct after Philadelphia police responded to reports of a disturbance on the 1200 block of Filbert Street, according to WPVI/Action News. Officers said she ignored multiple commands to move out of the robot's path.
The confrontation drew online attention and raised questions about where protest rights end and criminal obstruction begins.
Video of the incident circulated online, according to WPVI/Action News. Police said witnesses reported the disturbance before officers arrived.

Avride's sidewalk robots are a small but visible part of Uber Eats' Center City delivery network, operating under Pennsylvania state oversight.

Background (Delivery robot, Wikipedia):
A delivery robot is an autonomous robot that provides "last mile" delivery services. Delivery robots have been used in food delivery, package delivery, hospital delivery, and room service.

Background (Technological unemployment, Wikipedia):
Technological unemployment is the loss of jobs due to technological change. It is a key type of structural unemployment. Technological change typically includes the introduction of labour-saving "mechanical-muscle" machines or more efficient "mechanical-mind" processes (automation) and, in doing so, humans' role in these processes are minimized. Historical examples include artisan weavers losing work due to the introduction of mechanized looms, leading to protests by the Luddites. A contemporary example of technological unemployment is the displacement of retail cashiers by self-service tills and cashierless stores.

text:
Police just handcuffed a 78-year-old woman for standing in front of a delivery robot.

She stood on a Philadelphia sidewalk to protest machines taking human delivery jobs.

The legal charge is where this gets weird.

Carolyn Marvin, a retired University of Pennsylvania professor, repeatedly stepped in front of an Uber Eats robot on Filbert Street. Cops asked her to move multiple times. When she refused, they put her in cuffs for disorderly conduct.

Marvin says blocking the machines is her First Amendment right to protest technological unemployment in public space.

The technology and state regulations are now colliding on public footpaths:
• Avride robots travel at up to 5 mph using lidar and cameras
• Pennsylvania state law mandates that the robots yield to pedestrians
• Operator violations carry fines from $25 to $1,000

Yet when a human forces the robot to yield, the human gets arrested.

Other residents have kicked, toppled, or blocked the fleet since it launched in Center City. But this arrest sets a clear precedent.

My read: automation is moving out of software and onto municipal concrete.

When police enforce a robot's delivery route over a citizen's protest, corporate algorithms have officially secured public right-of-way.

Will your city prioritize pedestrian protest or autonomous delivery?

Source: The Verge, with reporting from New York Post and The Sun
